generated_text: Speaker_1: … honestly, I just think Darren’s mum is getting worse. Not deliberately, you understand, but she *always* manages to steer the conversation back to how wonderful *her* grandchildren are. It’s exhausting. And little Leo was trying so hard to show her his building blocks! Speaker_2: (Chuckles, gently bouncing the baby on her knee) Oh, bless him. And bless you for enduring it. Mothers, eh? They're a force of nature. At least you had a nice night out with Sarah on Friday, though? You needed it. Distraction therapy. Speaker_1: It was lovely, actually. Proper belly laughs. We went to that new Italian place on the Parade. Remember I mentioned it? The one with the fairy lights? The pasta was…well, let’s just say I’m regretting the extra garlic bread this morning. Worth it, though. It’s just… a bit lonely sometimes, isn’t it? Everyone else seems to be doing these amazing trips, spontaneous weekends… and I’m just… here. Speaker_2: Here, holding down the fort, being a brilliant aunt and keeping *my* life vaguely organised while I flap about! You’re not ‘just here’, love. You’re amazing. And honestly, those Instagram versions of everyone's lives are mostly lies. Sarah probably didn’t mention the argument she had with her husband about leaving the washing up until Monday? Speaker_1: (Sighs) Probably not. You’re right. Still…seeing her photos from Cornwall…makes you wonder. Anyway, enough about my pathetic wanderlust. How's work going? Still buried under proofreading reports? Speaker_2: Buried, absolutely buried. I've got that massive academic paper to turn around by Thursday. Honestly, the footnotes alone are a novel. It pays the bills, though, doesn’t it? And it lets me spend time with this little one. (Kisses the baby’s head) She’s growing so fast. Honestly, she was tiny last week, and now she’s grabbing at everything. Speaker_1: She is! She's a proper little character. I can’t believe she's almost six months already. It feels like only yesterday we were all gathered at your place, waiting for the announcement. Do you think… do you think we should start thinking about a little party for her half-birthday? Speaker_2: Ooh, that's a good idea! A little milestone celebration. Nothing huge, just family. We could do it here? Your garden's bigger, which is useful for crawling chaos. Speaker_1: Yes, absolutely. We could get a little cake… not too much sugar, obviously. And maybe some balloons. Oh, and I’ll need to book some time off work, which is a nightmare at the moment. I’ve got that website copy to finish for Mrs. Peterson, and she’s *very* particular about font choices. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, Mrs. Peterson. The font queen! You have the patience of a saint dealing with her. Right, okay, half-birthday party. Let’s pencil in the 27th? That gives us a couple of weeks to organise. We need to ring Mum and Dad, too. They’ll be buzzing to hear about it. Speaker_1: Perfect. The 27th sounds good. And yes, Mum and Dad will be thrilled. They've been wanting to visit ever since they heard about her rolling over. They’re convinced she’s a prodigy, you know. Speaker_2: (Smiling) That’s our Mum and Dad. Everything’s extraordinary. Speaking of visits… I was thinking about taking the girls to see Auntie Carol next month. She’s been a bit down since Uncle George… well, you know. Speaker_1: That’s a lovely idea. She’ll really appreciate it. The girls adore her. Just… maybe warn them about the cat. Mr. Bigglesworth is a bit of a menace. He tried to steal Isabelle’s biscuit last time. Speaker_2: Noted!

Speaker_1: … honestly, the sheer *volume* of paperwork they wanted for Bailey, even with the pet passport, was unbelievable. You’d think they’d suspect I was smuggling something more than a slightly anxious Border Terrier. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, taking a sip of his pint) Right? It’s like they actively *want* to discourage tourism. Remember when we did the Interrail thing after uni? It was relatively painless, even hopping between France, Germany and Italy. Now? It sounds like applying for a visa to North Korea. Speaker_1: Exactly! I was telling Mam about it, and she was saying even back in the seventies, travelling to Spain with the kids was less hassle. And that was *before* passports were even standard for everyone in the EU! The assumption now is guilt until proven innocence, isn’t it? "Right, where are your stamps? Your proof of onward travel? Your financial statements?" It's exhausting. Speaker_2: It's the mindset, I think. Pre-Brexit, there was a level of trust, a shared understanding. Now it feels…hostile. I’m thinking about taking the research to Barcelona next year for that conference, and I’m already dreading the airport. I used to just *go*. Speaker_1: Oh, Barcelona's lovely! We went a couple of years ago, before everything got… complicated. I’m heading to Amsterdam next month for a different project, and I’m genuinely considering flying into Schiphol and then getting the Eurostar to Brussels, just to avoid UK passport control altogether on the return. Sounds mental, doesn't it? Speaker_2: Not at all. That's clever, actually. A bit of a detour, but worth it if it saves you a three-hour queue and a grilling. I heard stories of people being turned away for slightly wonky passport photos. *Slightly* wonky! Speaker_1: Don’t even. My auntie nearly missed her flight to Portugal because her photo had a tiny bit of shadow. A tiny bit! She’s a solicitor, for goodness sake, she knows how to follow instructions. It’s just… deliberately obtuse. Do you think it’ll ever go back to how it was? Speaker_2: (Sighs) I’m not optimistic, to be honest. Politically, it's all… mess. Even if things *do* soften, the bureaucracy is there now. They've built the infrastructure for this level of scrutiny. It becomes self-perpetuating, you know? Speaker_1: Aye, I do. It feels like we’ve lost something precious. Little things, like just deciding on a whim to drive down to France for a weekend. That spontaneity is gone. It's all planning and permits and potential problems. Speaker_2: Remember that drive to Bruges we did? Didn’t even book accommodation, just rocked up and found a little B&B. Now, you’d need to book six months in advance, have proof of where you’re staying every night, and a detailed itinerary. Honestly, who wants a holiday that feels like filling out a tax return? Speaker_1: (Laughs) Exactly! It’s all a bit grim, isn’t it? I miss the easiness of it. I was hoping to do a cycling trip through the Netherlands next spring, but now I'm wondering if the stress is worth it. Maybe I'll stick to the Lake District. Less faff, better weather… probably. Speaker_2: The Lakes are good, yeah. Bit grey maybe, but good. But don’t give up on the Netherlands entirely. If you really want to go, we’ll research it together. We can be bureaucratic ninjas, prepping everything to within an inch of its life. It’s a testament to our education, isn't it? We can navigate complex systems… born out of needless complexity. Speaker_1: (Smiling) You're a good man, Liam. Bureaucratic ninjas. I like that. Alright, let's do that. A little bit of planning, a little bit of defiance, and a whole

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the whole point of shortbread is *butter*. Proper butter. Not that spreadable stuff. It needs to almost crumble when you bite into it, you know? Like little sandy castles. Remember Grandma’s? Speaker_2: (Small voice) Grandma’s was the best. She put sprinkles on sometimes. Pink ones. Speaker_1: She did! She was a bit of a rebel with the sprinkles, your Grandma. Your Dad used to get so cross she wasn’t sticking to the “classic” recipe. Though he ate plenty of them, I can assure you. Speaker_3: (Loudly) Can we *please* go back to Monopoly now? I need more money! Barnaby stole all my hotels! Speaker_1: (Sighs playfully) Barnaby, Barnaby, Barnaby. Always trying to bankrupt his sister. We’ll go back to Monopoly in a minute, love. We were just talking about desserts. Imagine a shortbread, lovely and buttery, *with* pink sprinkles… Speaker_2: Ooh! And chocolate! Can we have chocolate with the shortbread? Speaker_1: We could. Though I was thinking more of a nice raspberry jam. Or maybe even a lemon curd. Something a little bit tangy to cut through the richness. Speaker_3: Tangy? What’s tangy? Is that like…sour? I don't want sour. I want money! I landed on Mayfair and Barnaby *still* won't give me any. He said it’s ‘tactical’. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Tactical. He's learning all the right words, isn’t he? It means he’s clever, trying to win. Look, Barnaby, you can be tactical *and* fair. You can’t just refuse to pay rent. That’s not how Monopoly works. It's a basic principle of economics, really! Supply and demand, property ownership... Speaker_2: Economics? Is that like Maths? I hate Maths. Speaker_1: It’s… a bit like Maths, darling. It's about how things work with money, and what people want. Monopoly is actually a really good way to learn about it. See, you're learning even when you think you're just having fun! It teaches you about saving, investing… and the hardship of landing on Park Lane with a hotel! Speaker_3: But it’s NOT fair! He keeps buying all the orange ones! He said they're the best because everyone lands on them. Speaker_1: He’s right to think that, actually. Statistically, the orange properties are landed on more often. It's not cheating, it’s strategy. Though… (Looks pointedly at Barnaby) you could maybe be a *little* more generous. Remember, the point isn’t just to make everyone else go bankrupt. It's to have a bit of fun. Speaker_2: Can *I* buy some orange ones next time? Speaker_1: Absolutely. We'll all take turns being the property moguls. Right, okay, dessert decisions on hold for a minute. Everyone needs a little refuelling before another round of ruthless property acquisition. How about we each have a biscuit – not shortbread yet, we’ll save that for later – and then back to the game? Speaker_3: (Jumping up and down) Yes! And can I have the £500 note? I really need it! Speaker_1: (Smiling) We’ll see. First, a biscuit, then a sensible discussion about the distribution of capital. Honestly, sometimes I feel like I’m running a miniature bank here.

Speaker_1: … honestly, it’s just the principle of it, innit? Like, they *knew* I was starting this new job, and they decide *now* is the time to spring this on me about needing to sort out Grandad’s house? Right before my probation period even finishes? Speaker_2: (Sighing, adjusting the rearview mirror) Yeah, that’s… not ideal timing, is it? Your Auntie Brenda’s always been a bit… strategically unhelpful, hasn’t she? It’s like she enjoys creating chaos. Speaker_1: Strategic is a polite way of putting it. It’s flat-out passive aggressive! She could’ve mentioned this weeks ago. “Oh, just a little thing, your Grandad left everything to both of you, but the house needs a proper clear-out and you’re both responsible.” Like it's a jumble sale, not someone’s *life* we’re going through! Speaker_2: Well, probate can be a bit of a nightmare anyway. It's just the legal stuff takes ages. But yeah, springing it on you now... she definitely could’ve given you a heads-up. Did she at least offer to help? Speaker_1: Help? Ha! She said, and I quote, "Well, you’re the organised one, love. You’ll know what to do." Organised doesn’t mean I have magical time-bending powers, Brenda! I'm literally building a searchable database of historical linguistic data for a university project. It’s not exactly a skill transferable to decluttering forty years’ worth of Grandad’s hoarding. Speaker_2: (Chuckles gently) Right. Because comparing Old English verb conjugations to collectible biscuit tins is a perfectly logical leap. Look, how much stuff are we talking? Is it genuinely a full house, or just a few boxes in the attic? Speaker_1: A *full* house. He didn’t throw *anything* away. Old newspapers, broken radios, three different sets of encyclopaedias… I swear he had a collection of every promotional pen he ever received. And it all smells faintly of Woodbine and mothballs. Speaker_2: Oh, lovely. Sounds… charming. Okay, look, maybe we can break it down. We don’t have to do it all in one go. What about a weekend? We can block out a Saturday and a Sunday, get some skip bags, and just… attack it. We can order pizza, put some music on. It’ll be grim, but we’ll get through it. Speaker_1: (Slightly softening) That… actually doesn’t sound awful. Having someone else there to, you know, witness the sheer scale of the madness will be helpful. And someone to argue with Brenda on my behalf if she starts offering unhelpful "suggestions" over the phone. Speaker_2: Consider me your Brenda shield. I’m pretty good at politely but firmly shutting down unsolicited advice. Though, considering your Auntie Brenda, it might require a slightly less polite approach. Speaker_1: You’re the best, you know that? Seriously. I was getting so worked up about it, thinking I’d have to do it all on my own while juggling everything else. It’s just… Grandad meant a lot to me, and it feels disrespectful to just rush through it all. Speaker_2: I know he did. And rushing isn't the answer. It’s about honouring his memory, not just getting the house cleared. And, look, on a practical level, the quicker we get it sorted, the quicker you can relax and focus on your probation. Besides, maybe we’ll find some hidden treasure amongst all the biscuit tins. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Don’t get my hopes up. Though a first edition Beano would be a good find. Alright, operation “Grandad’s House” is a go. This weekend? Speaker_2: This weekend. We’ll face the mothballs together. And I'll bring gloves. Lots of gloves.

Speaker_1: …No, I’m tellin’ ya, the council’s gone soft. Absolutely soft. Back in my day, if a hedge was overhandin’ onto the pavement, you got a letter, plain as day. Nowt like this dithering about. Old Man Hemmings’ blackthorn’s practically blockin’ the whole bloomin’ path! Speaker_2: (Chuckles, a dry rasping sound) Ditherin’ is right, Arthur. Ditherin’ sums ‘em up nicely. Remember when they tried to put a roundabout on Dereham Road? An absolute shambles, that was. Spent a fortune, didn’t they? And it made things worse! Speaker_3: Oh, don't even *start* me on Dereham Road. I used to take little Timmy down there to the park, and it was a nightmare. Always queued for ages. Though, to be fair, it *is* busier now than it used to be. All that new buildin' up towards Weston Longville. Speaker_1: That’s just it, isn’t it, Margaret? More people, more problems. But they don’t seem to be spendin’ the money *wisely*. They’re puttin’ cycle lanes everywhere nobody uses. Cycle lanes! In Norfolk! Who’s gonna cycle in this weather? Speaker_2: (Scoffs) Showin’ off, that’s what it is. Tryin’ to be all…progressive. Doesn’t work, though. Folk round here like their cars. Always ‘ave. My dad, he’d polish his Morris Minor every Sunday. Never seen anything like it. Speaker_3: Ernest, you and your cars! Remember when you tried to fix the exhaust on that Austin Cambridge yourself? Nearly set the garage alight! Speaker_2: (Grinning) Now, now, Margaret, a man’s gotta ‘ave a hobby. And it weren't *nearly* alight! Just a little…smoky. Besides, it saved a few bob. Everything costs a fortune these days, don’t it? Even a loaf of bread. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. The price of everything's gone through the roof. It’s a disgrace. And the television…all this talk of strikes. Nurses strikin’, train drivers strikin’. It’s enough to give you the heebie-jeebies. Speaker_3: It's awful, Arthur. They deserve a proper wage. Workin’ like that, lookin’ after people... it's not easy. I always had respect for nurses. Remember Mrs. Davies, when your mother was poorly? She was a saint. Speaker_1: Aye, a saint she were. Came round every day, bless her. Though, she did ‘ave a fondness for a little sherry, didn’t she? Didn’t mind a drop, that one. Speaker_2: (Laughing) You’re tellin’ me! She’d be round ‘ere lookin’ for a cuppa and a sneaky tipple. Good woman, though. Rest her soul. Seems like all the good ones are goin’. Speaker_3: It does, doesn’t it? Everything changes. Makes you think, though…we’ve seen a lot in our time, haven't we? From black and white televisions to…well, whatever all this modern stuff is. Speaker_1: A fair bit, aye. I remember when the Yare was teeming with boats, proper cargo boats. Now it’s just… pleasure cruisers. Everything’s gone a bit soft, like I said. Speaker_2: Progress, they call it. I’m not so sure. Sometimes I think we were better off with things simpler. A bit of hard work, a pint down the pub, and a good neighbour. That’s all you needed. Speaker_3: You’re right about the neighbours, Ernest. We don't *know* our neighbours anymore. Everyone keeps themselves to themselves. It's a shame, really.

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the packaging is *still* giving me grief. I thought sourcing recycled cardboard would be straightforward, but finding boxes that are the right dimensions for the serum bottles *and* don’t look completely… well, cheap, is proving a nightmare. Everything’s either too big, so you’ve got loads of void fill, or too small and you risk damage. Speaker_2: Ugh, packaging. The bane of my existence with the jewellery, honestly. It's always something. Did you actually measure the bottle dimensions precisely? Millimetre perfect? Because that’s what I had to do. I was sending out earrings in boxes that were, like, 2mm too short and they kept getting bent. Nightmare reviews. Speaker_1: I have! I’ve got a spreadsheet, naturally. Teacher brain, you see. Length, width, height, diameter of the dropper…the whole shebang. It's just… the off-the-shelf options are awful. I'm considering bespoke, but the quotes I've got are frankly terrifying. It would eat into the profit margin before we’ve even sold anything. Speaker_2: Bespoke is definitely pricey. Have you looked at eBay for bulk boxes? Sounds awful, I know, but sometimes you can find people clearing out stock and you get a decent deal. I got loads of little velvet pouches for the earrings there, proper cheap. Speaker_1: That’s a thought, actually. I’ve been so focused on ‘eco-friendly’ I’ve maybe overlooked practical cost-effectiveness. It’s just… the whole ‘Honest Skincare’ brand hinges on appearing really premium, but ethically sound. It's a fine line, isn't it? Speaker_2: It is! And I think people appreciate that you *are* trying with the eco-stuff. They’ll forgive a slightly less fancy box if they know you’re not just chucking everything in plastic. Speaking of which, how's the social media marketing going? Have you started running those Instagram ads we talked about? Speaker_1: Slowly. It’s all a learning curve. I did a little campaign targeting women aged 25-45 interested in organic skincare, but the click-through rate was pathetic. I think I need to refine the imagery. It’s all very… botanical and calm, but maybe a bit bland? Speaker_2: Bland is the enemy! People scroll so fast. You need something that *grabs* them. Maybe photos of real people using the serum? Before and after, you know? A bit of actual visible result. I find that works really well with the jewellery. Showing someone looking fabulous wearing it. Speaker_1: That’s good thinking. I've got my sister willing to be a guinea pig, she's got lovely skin anyway. Although she’ll want paying, naturally. Family discounts don’t exist, apparently. Speaker_2: (Laughs) Tell me about it! My cousin wanted a discount on a necklace, said it was for ‘exposure’ – exposure doesn’t pay the bills, love! Anyway, seriously, get some good photos. And think about reels. Short videos always do well. Speaker_1: I'm trying to learn TikTok, honestly. It feels… alien. I feel ancient even saying that! Anyway, enough about my struggles. How are things with the shop? Still manic? Speaker_2: Manic is an understatement. Wedding season is insane. Everyone wants custom jewellery. Mum’s helping me with some of the simpler stuff, which is a lifesaver. Speaking of which, are you still on for that weekend in Cornwall in September? We really need a break. Speaker_1: Oh, yes! Definitely. I’ve already requested the time off from school. It'll be bliss. We should start looking at cottages properly. Do you want sea views, or are we happy a little further inland? Somewhere with a decent kitchen is essential, I need to practice my baking. Speaker_2: Sea views are nice, but not essential. And yes, kitchen is key. I’m determined to learn how to make a proper Cornish pasty while we’re

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the sheer *audacity* of it! Claiming it was a ‘technical glitch’. A technical glitch that managed to misallocate funds to a company registered in the Cayman Islands? Don’t make me laugh, David. It’s blatant, isn't it? Just blatant. Speaker_2: (Sighing, stirring his tea) You’ve been reading too much of that online stuff, Margaret. Always gets you worked up. It’s probably just incompetence, you know? Bureaucracy gone wrong. They’re not all master criminals. Though, I’ll grant you, it *does* look a bit dodgy. Speaker_1: Incompetence on a scale that funnels money offshore? David, I taught history for thirty years! I've seen patterns, I recognize a cover-up when I see one. And did you hear what they’re doing with the NHS now? Allowing private companies to… well, effectively cherry-pick the easy cases. It's dismantling it, bit by bit. Speaker_2: Now, now. Don't get yourself going again. I read something about that too, but they said it’s to reduce waiting lists. Apparently, they’ll still treat everyone, just… differently. Streamlined, they called it. Speaker_1: Streamlined! It’s privatisation by stealth, that’s what it is. They’ll leave the NHS with all the complicated, expensive cases and the private sector will cream off the profitable ones. It's utterly immoral. And it’s all connected, you know. This corruption, this… erosion of public services. It’s all part of the same rotten system. Speaker_2: (Takes a sip of tea) You always see the worst in things, Margaret. It’s a gift, I suppose, being a historian. Always looking at the decline and fall. But sometimes things aren’t *that* bad. How are you feeling, actually? You’ve been quieter than usual these past few weeks. More… preoccupied. Speaker_1: (Looks out the window, a flicker of sadness crossing her face) Oh, just…thinking. About Mother, mostly. It's nearly the anniversary, you know. Twenty years next month. It still feels like yesterday sometimes, especially when I'm in the garden. She loved her roses. Speaker_2: I know. It does. I miss her terribly. She always had a kind word for everyone, didn’t she? And she made the best scones. Remember those? Light as a feather. Speaker_1: (A small smile plays on her lips) Oh, don't even mention the scones. I've tried for years to replicate them, and I’ve never quite managed it. It's a family secret, lost with her, I suppose. It's just… lonely, David. Being here. In the house. It's too quiet. Speaker_2: I know it is. Have you thought about joining that gardening club Mrs. Henderson mentioned? It might get you out a bit. And they're a friendly bunch, apparently. Speaker_1: Gardening club? (Scoffs gently) Surrounded by people discussing the latest slug pellets? Not particularly appealing, honestly. Though… I suppose it's better than staring at the four walls. It’s just… everything feels a bit pointless now. Teaching was my life. And now… now I just read the depressing news and watch the world go to pot. Speaker_2: You’re not pointless, Margaret. You’re my sister. And you were a fantastic teacher, you know that. Hundreds of kids benefited from your knowledge and patience. You made a difference. Don’t let the news convince you otherwise. Speaker_1: (Looks at David, her eyes softening) You always did know how to say the right thing, didn't you? Even when I’m being a miserable old Scot, grumbling about everything. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) That's my job, isn't it? To keep you grounded. And to make sure you have enough tea. Now, finish your cup. And perhaps we can watch that detective show you enjoy

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the sheer volume of Brussels sprouts my mother insists on making is criminal. It's not *Christmas* without them, apparently. Like a tradition carved in stone. Though, I suspect it’s less about tradition and more about her proving she can still ‘provide’ for everyone, you know? Speaker_2: Aye, I get that. Me mam's the same with the trifle. It’s always gotta be *her* trifle, even though no one really eats it. It’s just…there. Symbolism, I think. Though sprouts, aye, that’s a bit much. Still, beats having to pretend to enjoy Uncle Barry’s questionable Christmas pudding. Speaker_3: Oh god, the pudding. Last year it was… suspiciously bouncy. I think he added too much brandy *and* something else. Anyway, speaking of providing, have you sorted your heating, Liam? It’s freezing out there. This house is lovely, Esme, but the old stone walls… they just *suck* the heat. Speaker_4: (Chuckles) Tell me about it. Mine’s a converted barn. Romantic, yes. Efficient at retaining heat? Absolutely not. I’m burning through logs like it’s going out of fashion. Thinking about investing in one of those fancy log splitters. My axe arm is starting to protest. Speaker_1: Oh, good idea. Are you still making those incredible benches and tables, Rhys? I need a new small side table for the living room. Something… rustic, but not *too* rustic. And definitely sturdy enough to withstand clumsy postgraduate research habits. Speaker_4: Aye, still at it. Got a big commission for a pub table at the moment. Keeps me busy. Rustic’s my bread and butter, but I can do ‘refined rustic’ if that makes sense. I’ve got access to some lovely oak, or I could even work with walnut. What about you, Esme? How’s the research going? Still wrangling with those ancient texts? Speaker_1: Unfortunately. It's a bit of a slog, to be honest. Funding bids are the real killer, though. Feels like I spend more time writing proposals than actually…doing the research. It’s all a bit disheartening. Sometimes I fantasize about retiring to a cottage and growing mulberries. Utterly impractical, I know. Speaker_2: Retirement? You’re barely thirty! I’m already starting to have those thoughts though. This job’s alright, pays the bills, but staring at industrial machinery all day… it’s not exactly fulfilling is it? I’d rather be fixing things for people directly, maybe open a little repair shop. Speaker_3: That sounds brilliant, actually! A real community hub. I sometimes worry about what I'll do *after* the PhD. Academia is so competitive. It’s all publish or perish. The thought of endlessly applying for postdoc positions… it’s terrifying. Speaker_4: You’ll be alright, Beth. You’re a grafter. And you’ve got skills. Speaking of skills, anyone fancy a game of cards after dinner? I brought a new deck. Might be a good distraction from worrying about the future and rogue Christmas puddings. Speaker_1: Oh, yes please! I’m terrible at cards, but it's the taking part that counts. Though, Liam usually cleans us all out. He's got a face like a poker player, doesn't he? Speaker_2: (Grinning) It’s a gift. And I've had a bit of practice in the pub. Though, honestly, the real skill is knowing when to fold. Just like life, eh? Speaker_3: (Laughing) Very profound, Liam. Right, before we get too philosophical, does anyone want more wine? And maybe we should strategically position ourselves further away from the window, just in case that cold snap actually hits.

Speaker_1: … honestly, I just don’t understand why we have so many different forks. Like, seriously, four types of fork? What’s the point of a fish fork when you can just use a normal one? It’s ridiculous. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You're sounding like Dad, actually. He's always moaning about the cutlery drawer. Says Mum’s got a fork for *every* occasion. Speaker_3: Aye, well, yer Mam always liked to be prepared. It wasn’t about needing ‘em, it was about *having* ‘em. Represented a certain standard, didn’t it? You know, when we had guests… proper guests. Not just the usual lot. Speaker_4: She always worried about appearances, your mother. Never wanted to look… wanting. It stemmed from her childhood, I think. Things were tight then. She remembered not having a matching set, ever. Speaker_5: (Mumbling) Aye… tight. Used to use wooden spoons for everything, we did. Lucky to *have* cutlery, never mind a special fork for a kipper. Speaker_1: Right, okay, that's… a completely different perspective. I just thought it was excessive. I'm trying to declutter my flat, and this place is a goldmine of things I don’t need. Although, most of it is lovely, just... a lot. Speaker_2: You could ‘borrow’ some, you know, for when you have people round. Impress your mates with the fancy fork selection. Speaker_1: (Scoffs) They’d just think I’m weird. They eat pizza off paper plates, mostly. Speaking of guests, are we still on for Sarah and Ben next weekend? I haven’t heard anything confirmed. Speaker_3: I spoke to Sarah yesterday. She said Ben’s got a work thing, a training course or summat. They’re postponing it till the month after. Gutted, I was looking forward to seein’ ‘em. Haven't seen 'em since Christmas. Speaker_4: That’s a shame. Ben’s a good lad. Always polite. Reminds me a bit of… well, never mind. Speaker_5: (Quietly) Used to be good to have a house full of young ‘uns. Plenty of noise. Gets quiet, don’t it? Too quiet. Speaker_2: It does get quiet, Grandad. That’s why we try and come round as often as we can. Keeps things lively. Although, Mum's still trying to get me to marry Sophie's sister. She thinks they'd be a 'good match'. Speaker_1: (Raises an eyebrow) Oh, *really*? Is she still pushing that? She tried to set me up with the butcher’s son last time I was here! Speaker_3: Yer Mam’s a matchmaker at heart, loves it she does. Doesn't mean she's right, mind. Sophie’s sister's nice enough, but you’ve got to want it, haven’t you? Speaker_4: She means well, though. Sees you lot settling down, having families… it’s what she always wanted for us. Mum's already booked me a careers session. Apparently, they’ll tell me my ‘strengths and weaknesses’. As if I don't already know I'm good at art and terrible at public speaking. Speaker_1: Oh god, don't even mention public speaking. The thought makes me sweat. Did you finish that Food Tech practical? The one with the soufflés? Speaker_2: Thankfully! It was a disaster. Mine collapsed before I even took it out of the oven. Mrs. Peterson said it was “a learning experience”. A learning experience in soufflé failure, maybe. Yours looked amazing though, all puffy and golden. Speaker_1: That was luck, pure and simple. I think the oven was just being nice to me for once. Speaker_1: … honestly, darling, all these superhero films, they just all blur into one, don't they? Bang, pow, someone flies, another one's got a metal suit - it’s just *noise*. Speaker_2: I haven't seen that one. I’ll add it to my list. Look, let's just agree to disagree about superheroes. But Asteroid City? What do you say? It’s a bit quiet then. Speaker_1: Tuesday sounds lovely. Gives me time to prepare myself for…fussiness. And maybe have a little nap beforehand. These modern films, they’re exhausting just *thinking* about them.

Speaker_1: … honestly, Mum, the traffic was *awful* getting up here. Absolutely gridlocked on the M40. I swear, every time I come to Birmingham it’s the same. Speaker_2: The train’s alright, but it's not the same, is it? No freedom. And it’s not cheap, is it? Especially now. Everything’s going up, isn't it? Even a simple cup of coffee. I’m hoping for a pay rise this year, though. It's getting… tight. Especially with saving for a deposit on a place. Speaker_2: A pay rise is what you deserve! You work your socks off. And saving… well, good luck with that these days. Property prices are ridiculous. Remember when we bought this house? A fraction of what they are now. Though, I suppose wages were different then too. Are you still walking Buster when it’s pouring? Speaker_1: Yes, poor thing demands his walk, rain or shine. He's getting on a bit now, though. His joints aren’t what they used to be. He's a proper old man dog. I've been thinking about getting him one of those little ramps for the sofa. Speaker_2: Oh, a ramp! That’s a lovely idea. He’d appreciate that. He’s a good dog, that Buster. I always enjoy seeing him. Did you see the football on Saturday? Aston Villa actually won! Speaker_1: I did! I managed to catch the highlights. I’m not a massive football fan, but even *I* was pleased for you. You were practically doing cartwheels! Speaker_2: (chuckles) Well, it doesn't happen often, does it? It’s a bit of a lifeline, watching them win. Keeps me going through the week, it does. Court was… interesting today. A nasty little dispute over a will. All about money, of course. Same old story. Speaker_1: Sounds stressful. You must see everything, working there. Does it ever… get to you? Speaker_2: It does. Some days are worse than others. You learn to detach, I suppose. But it’s hard, seeing people at their lowest. Anyway, enough of that grimness. We were talking plans. Are you free next weekend? I was thinking we could go to the botanical gardens. It’s supposed to be lovely this time of year. Speaker_1: That sounds wonderful, Mum. I'd love that. I really need a bit of a recharge. And, actually, I was hoping to pick your brain about something. There's a case I was reading about for a CPD course – a wrongful dismissal claim – and you’ve always had such a good understanding of the law, even without being a solicitor. Speaker_2: Oh, go on then. Lay it on me. I’ve heard enough in that courtroom to fill a textbook. Although, don’t expect anything fancy! It’s just common sense, mostly. Now, tell me what’s troubling you…and I’ll get

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the student feedback was *brutal*. Apparently, my lecture on post-structuralism was “too much, too soon” for a Tuesday afternoon. Can you believe it? Too much Derrida before coffee, apparently. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, bless them. They do say timing is everything. Though, if they can’t handle a bit of deconstruction before 2pm, are they *really* ready for university? Still, brutal feedback isn’t fun. Did you at least get some constructive criticism mixed in with the negativity? Speaker_1: A couple. Someone said my pacing was good, which is a win. But mostly it was just… bewildered emojis. It’s hard adapting to how they learn here, isn’t it? Different expectations. Back in Norwich, I could throw around Foucault and they’d at least *pretend* to understand. Speaker_2: It's a completely different cultural approach to learning. Much more emphasis on rote memorisation, less on critical thinking, generally. Though, I've found that once you break through that, they’re incredibly engaged. My history class is slowly, finally, starting to question sources. Small victories. Speaker_1: That’s good to hear. It feels like pushing uphill sometimes. Oh! Speaking of uphill battles… did you manage to find those weirdly specific tea towels I asked about? The ones with the vintage botanical illustrations? Speaker_2: (Sighs dramatically) That was an *adventure*. You know, this city is amazing for everything… except obscure British household goods. I went to three different markets. The first one just had knock-off football shirts. The second had…well, I’m still not entirely sure *what* the second one had. A lot of plastic, that’s all I’ll say. Speaker_1: Oh, you poor thing! I should have just ordered them online. But I thought it might be nice to support the local economy. Always a noble but ultimately disastrous plan, isn’t it? Speaker_2: Exactly. Eventually, I found a tiny shop hidden down a side street – run by an expat Scot, of all people. He had one set. *One*. And he’d priced them like they were made of gold. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Honestly! Only in China. How much were they? Speaker_2: Don’t ask. Let’s just say I paid more than they’d cost at John Lewis. But I have them. They’re safe. I’m bringing them home with me. We can have a proper English tea tomorrow, with botanical glory. Speaker_1: You are a lifesaver! Honestly, you’re the best. I’ve been craving a proper cuppa. This jasmine tea is lovely, but it’s just not the same, is it? It lacks… robustness. Speaker_2: Robustness. That’s the word. And speaking of bringing things home, I promised Old Man Wei I’d pick up some of those British biscuits he loves. Shortbread, specifically. Do we have any? Speaker_1: I think there's a half-empty tin in the kitchen. He'll be thrilled. He always asks about the weather in London, too. He truly believes it’s permanently shrouded in fog. Speaker_2: (Smiling) It’s a very romantic notion for him. He remembers London from the 70s, I think. Everything is exaggerated after fifty years. We should invite him and Mrs. Li for dinner next week. It’s been ages. Speaker_1: Good idea. I’ll check my schedule tomorrow. We can do something easy. Roast chicken, maybe? And, naturally, served on the aggressively expensive botanical tea towels.

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the whole thing with Mrs. Peterson cancelling her book club because of her hair appointment is just *bonkers*. Like, a hair appointment trumps Jane Austen? Really? Speaker_2: (Small voice) Is Jane Austen about princesses? Speaker_1: (Smiling, stirring something in a bowl) Not exactly princesses, love. It’s about people, and love, and… complicated families. A bit like ours, actually! Though hopefully with fewer arguments about who gets the last biscuit. Speaker_3: (Bolting into the kitchen, clutching a dinosaur) I want a biscuit! Is it chocolate chip? Speaker_1: Not yet, darling. These are for the photoshoot. Remember? We’re trying to make them look *really* nice. Auntie Sarah wants pictures for her website. Speaker_2: Photoshoot? Will I have to wear the sparkly dress? Speaker_1: Possibly! It’s a very sparkly dress. But we can talk about that later. Right now, I need to figure out Saturday. I promised Chloe I’d try and meet her in Cambridge, but if I’m baking *and* trying to get you two presentable for photos… Speaker_3: I *am* presentable! Roar! (Strikes a dinosaur pose) Speaker_1: (Chuckles) You’re a very presentable dinosaur, yes. But Auntie Sarah wants… less dinosaur, perhaps. Look, I was thinking I could drop you two with Gran and Grandad on Saturday morning. Would you like that? Speaker_2: Can we read with Grandad? He does funny voices. Speaker_1: You absolutely can. He promised to do the Gruffalo. And then I can nip into town and see Chloe. We haven't properly chatted since… well, since forever. She’s just started a new pottery class and apparently, it’s all going brilliantly. Speaker_3: Pottery sounds messy. Can we make pottery later? Speaker_1: Maybe, after the photoshoot. And *after* a very thorough clean-up. Okay, so Gran and Grandad on Saturday morning. That leaves the afternoon for baking and… hair. Oh goodness, the hair. Freddie, yours is looking a bit wild. Speaker_3: It's aerodynamic for dinosaur flying! Speaker_1: (Laughing) That’s… a very good point. But Auntie Sarah might not appreciate the aerodynamic look. Lily, have you been brushing yours? Speaker_2: Mummy brushed it this morning. But it got messy when I was pretending to be Rapunzel. Speaker_1: (Sighs playfully) Naturally. Right. Maybe a quick trim for both of you after baking? There’s that little salon in the village, they're usually good with wiggly children. Although… I really need a haircut too. It's getting down to my eyes. Speaker_3: You look like a lion! Roar! Speaker_1: (Waving a wooden spoon) Very funny. Look, let's focus on the cookies for now. Can you two help me sprinkle the chocolate chips? And *no* eating them before they're baked, understood? I'm making a shepherd’s pie for dinner, too. Your favourite! Speaker_2: With the mashed potato stars? Speaker_1: The very best mashed potato stars. It's going to be a busy Saturday, isn’t it? But a good busy. We’ll have seen friends, made cookies, possibly had haircuts, and hopefully… got some nice photos. Speaker_3: And read the Gruffalo! Speaker_1: (Smiling warmly) And read the Gruffalo. Definitely. Now, chocolate chips… carefully!

Speaker_1: … honestly, the library's just *packed* now. Like, every single desk is taken. It’s a proper scrum, innit? I tried to find a quiet corner to do my essay on Victorian literature and ended up practically nose-to-nose with someone eating a pot noodle. The *smell*, Liv, the smell! Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, bless you. Sounds charming. Kingston library is always a bit… intense. Especially around deadline time. Mine’s not much better, to be fair. Though, at least I can usually snag a table if I go super early. Like, before nine. Are you actually making any progress on that essay, though? Victorian lit sounds…dense. You can't just binge-read critical analysis. Plus, Mum keeps texting me about what I'm having for dinner when I go home next weekend. It's distracting! She wants to know if I’m eating enough vegetables. Honestly, like I’m five. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Mums, eh? Mine’s the same! Constantly asking if I’m wearing enough layers. She's convinced I'm always cold, even in summer. But yeah, that essay sounds rough. Honestly, I'm just trying to get through this statistics module. It's killing me softly. I just don’t *get* standard deviation. It feels like they’re just making numbers up. Speaker_1: Oh god, statistics. I steered well clear of that. Smart move, I reckon. Listen, are you free later? I was thinking we could grab some drinks – not loads, just a couple – at The Fighting Cocks. They’ve got that student discount on Tuesdays. Might take the edge off this uni stress. Speaker_2: Ooh, that actually sounds amazing. I'm definitely in need of a de-stress. I think I officially lost a brain cell trying to understand confidence intervals. What are you thinking of getting? They do a pretty good mojito, although it's a bit pricey even *with* the discount. Speaker_1: Mojito sounds good. Or maybe just a simple gin and tonic. Need something that won't lead to a maths-induced meltdown. Oh! Speaking of drinks, remember Uncle Barry’s attempt at making cocktails at Christmas? Honestly, it was like someone mixed paint stripper and lemonade. Speaker_2: (Bursting out laughing) Oh my *god*, yes! And he was so proud of them! He kept offering everyone “Barry’s Special”. I think I politely pretended to drink it and then tipped it into the plant. It probably explained why Auntie Carol’s fern died a week later. Speaker_1: (Laughing too) No way! That’s brilliant! Honestly, he's a legend. So, The Fighting Cocks then? Say, sevenish? Gives me enough time to *attempt* another paragraph on Mr. Rochester being a bit of a dodgy bloke. Speaker_2: Perfect. Seven’s good. I’ll finish up these notes – or at least *look* like I'm finishing these notes – and meet you there. Oh, and I'm starving. This canteen food is grim, honestly. That pasta bake looks like it’s been sitting under a heat lamp since last Tuesday. Speaker_1: Tell me about it! I just picked at a salad because I felt vaguely guilty about the lack of greens in my life, as Mum would say. Maybe The Fighting Cocks does a decent portion of chips. That’s a nutritional food group, right? Speaker_2: Absolutely. Chips are basically vegetables. Don’t let anyone tell you otherwise. Right, gotta get back to the statistical nightmares. See you later! Speaker_1: See ya! And may the odds be ever in your favour with standard deviation. You'll need it.

Speaker_1: … honestly, I just think people get too obsessed with all-inclusive. Like, you *have* to explore! You’re in Greece, for goodness sake, not Blackpool. It wasn't *that* bad. And I did carry most of the water. Besides, I’ve been going to the gym, alright? Trying to, anyway. Work's been relentless. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. All the tension of a high-stakes drama, but with more wellies and bad sweaters. Honestly, I’m hooked. And the commentary. The bloke sounds like he’s reporting on the Champions League final. “And here we see young Barry, reeling in a magnificent… whiting!” Speaker_2: (Laughing) You’re pulling my leg! That sounds brilliantly awful. I’ve been trying to get through ‘Severance’ – everyone keeps saying it’s amazing, but it’s so… slow. Speaker_3: ‘Severance’ is good, you just need to persevere. Mam's got enthusiastic, bless her. She sees something on telly and thinks she’s a Michelin-star chef. We ended up ordering a takeaway. Indian, naturally. Can't go wrong with a good curry. Speaker_2: You know, we should all get together for a proper meal soon. Not a dodgy paella experiment. Maybe next weekend? I could attempt a Shepherd’s Pie. I'm surprisingly good at it, if I do say so myself. Speaker_3: Shepherd’s Pie sounds perfect. I'll bring the wine. And maybe a hazard suit, just in case we suspect any accidental raisin deployment. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Deal. And I’ll make sure to download a few episodes of ‘The Reeling’ for post-dinner entertainment. You have been warned. Though, honestly, you *have* to see it to believe it. It's utterly bonkers.

Speaker_1: …No, no, I’m tellin’ ya, the traffic was *shockin’*. Shockin’. Reminds me of when we took the Morris Minor to London back in ‘68. Everything’s digital, instant. They used to come to me needing help with their homework, now they just Google it. Speaker_1: Google. Blast it all. I tried to sell that old gramophone on eBay last week. Took me hours to work out how to photograph it right. And then some fella offered me a fiver! A *fiver*! For a perfectly good gramophone. Speaker_2: Five pounds? That’s outrageous! You should've ignored him. I sold my china cabinet on there, got a decent price. Though, getting it delivered was a nightmare. Had to help the poor delivery man, bless him. He nearly threw his back out. Speaker_3: Speaking of selling things, have you two given any more thought to downsizing? Speaker_2: Right, point taken. I’ll add it to the ever-growing list of things I need to do. Speaking of lists, have you guys sorted the white goods for the new place, Chloe? Are you keeping your washing machine? Speaker_1: I'm selling it actually. It’s a bit old and honestly, it makes a racket. I was looking at getting an integrated one, something quieter. But they’re surprisingly expensive. I might have to stick with a standard one for now. Speaker_3: Oh, integrated ones are lovely, but a complete waste of money, in my opinion. You don't *see* it most of the time, do you? Just get a good, reliable model. You don’t need all the bells and whistles. It’s the same with dishwashers, honestly. Speaker_2: I’m with Kerrie on this one. A good dishwasher is a life saver. Especially with all the cooking you do. How was that pottery class you were telling us about, by the way? Did you manage to make anything resembling a pot? Speaker_1: (Laughs) It was… an experience. Let’s just say my “pot” looked more like a wonky ashtray. But it was really fun, and the instructor was lovely. I might sign up for another one, though I think I need to

Speaker_1: … honestly, Mum, it’s just *bonkers* out here. Look at this queue. What’s even happening up ahead? Just a solid wall of red lights. Speaker_2: (Sighs) Standard Friday afternoon, darling. Heading towards the North Circular is always a gamble. You shouldn’t have offered to drive me to collect Auntie Maureen’s things, really. Should’ve just got a cab. Speaker_1: No way, wouldn’t hear of it. You were stressing about getting everything sorted and I had the day free after lectures. Besides, it’s good to catch up, innit? Even if it’s stuck in traffic. So, how *is* Auntie Maureen, really? You sounded a bit… vague on the phone. Speaker_2: She’s… declining, love. It’s not sudden, it's just… a gradual fading. She's mostly confused these days. That’s why she wants me to have her books, you know. She keeps saying ‘they need a good home.’ It's mostly first editions, actually. A few proper gems. Speaker_1: Wow. First editions! That's… amazing. She always did have good taste. Bit of a hoarder though, wasn't she? Remember that time we tried to clear out her attic and found fifteen identical porcelain cats? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Don’t remind me. Nearly gave your father a heart attack. Speaking of which, have you told him about… well, about the potential manuscript I’m looking at? The one from the French writer? Speaker_1: Oh yeah, vaguely. You mentioned it. Something about a post-war romance? Is it good? You were sounding pretty excited. Speaker_2: It *is* good, actually. Really good. But it’s a problem. The author wants to go entirely digital. No print run. Just ebook. And the *TLS* are adamant they won’t review anything that isn’t available in hard copy. It’s this ridiculous battle, isn’t it? Print versus digital. I feel like a dinosaur sometimes. Speaker_1: That *is* a pickle. Though, honestly, I get both sides. I read most of my course material online now, it’s just… easier. But there’s something about holding a real book, you know? That smell, the weight of it… Speaker_2: Exactly! And the prestige of a physical review! It's about permanence, darling. Digital’s so… fleeting. Although, on the flip side, it means fewer trees get chopped down. It's complicated. This author, Jean-Luc… he’s got a real story, though. Lived through the Liberation of Paris, you know? Speaker_1: No way! That’s mental. He must be… ancient. Speaker_2: Ninety-two! And sharp as a tack. He emailed me directly, which is unheard of. Usually, it’s agents and publishers. He insists he simply doesn’t *believe* in paper anymore. He said it represents a bygone era. Speaker_1: Stubborn old sod, then. Still, sounds like a good story. Look, we’re barely moving. Honestly, that bloke in the van over there is giving me serious road rage vibes. Speaker_4: (Snorting with laughter) Oh, Leo! You’re a disaster. A beautiful, chaotic disaster. Was the paella at least good *before* it made you question your life choices? Turns out, I left it at a bar after attempting a very embarrassing rendition of *Livin’ on a Prayer*. The bartender remembered me, thankfully. He was very amused. It choked us all out. And the ranger was fuming. Speaker_4: Ben was convinced he was Bear Grylls. He was definitely *not* Bear Grylls. He just smelled like burnt paper and disappointment. Speaker_2: (Raising his glass) To bad camping trips, questionable paella, and pigeons with a taste for chips! May our holidays always be slightly disastrous. Speaker_1: Hear, hear! And to avoiding Venice. Maybe.

**Speaker_1:** ...Honestly, the condensation inside the tent was biblical. Absolutely biblical. Woke up feeling like I'd been swimming, not sleeping. Last time, near Dartmoor, I had a stag practically breathing down my neck, curious as anything. **Speaker_2:** A stag! Alistair, you’re courting disaster! Honestly, you should be taking someone with you. Especially these days. I know you're fit as a fiddle for your age, but you can’t be gallivanting around the moors on your own. What if you’d fallen and broken something? **Speaker_1:** (Waves his hand dismissively) Nonsense, Elspeth. I’m perfectly capable. I’ve been doing this for years. And I *tell* people where I’m going, obviously. But it’s the solitude, you see. It clears the head. All this research… it gets a bit overwhelming sometimes. Staring at data all day. This…this is an antidote. **Speaker_3:** I think Mum’s got a point about safety, though. Even a seasoned camper can run into trouble. We had a student last year twist her ankle badly on a seemingly harmless path. It took us ages to get her down. And the signal out there is patchy at best. **Speaker_1:** It’s a calculated risk, Calum. Everything is. Look, I'm not suggesting everyone should be out there battling the elements. But for me, it’s profoundly restorative. The way the light changes on the snow, the sound of the wind… it’s a different level of immersion in nature than just a weekend walk. It’s almost…meditative. **Speaker_2:** Meditative and hypothermic, more like! Seriously though, the psychological benefits *do* make sense. Being disconnected, forced to simplify your needs… it’s like a primal reset. I see similar effects with patients who practice mindful walking, though without the risk of frostbite. It’s about finding that stillness, isn't it? **Speaker_3:** Exactly. And I think that’s why it’s gaining popularity, even amongst the younger generation. They’re so bombarded with stimulation, they crave that disconnect. Though they probably expect a gourmet hot chocolate afterwards. **Speaker_1:** (Scoffs) Gourmet hot chocolate! In my day, it was a lukewarm cup of tea and a biscuit, if you were lucky! Still, even that tastes extraordinary after a night under the stars. Listen, I’m planning another trip next month, maybe to the Brecon Beacons. **Speaker_2:** Oh, Alistair, don't even think about it. At least promise me you'll take a proper satellite phone, and let someone track your location. And a flask of something warming that *isn't* lukewarm tea! **Speaker_1:** (Grinning) I'll consider the satellite phone, just for you, Elspeth. But the tea

Speaker_1: …Aye, but that's what I’m sayin’, isn’t it? Like, everyone raves about *Dune*, right? Visually spectacular, all that. But when it comes down to it, the characters were just… flat. Proper cardboard cut-outs. Paul Atreides just mopes around bein’ special, and I didn't *feel* anything for ‘im, ya know? Not like with, say, Kvothe from *The Name of the Wind*. Speaker_2: (Chuckles lightly) Right, the classic Rothfuss debate. Though I think you're being a bit harsh on *Dune*. It’s less about individual character arcs and more about the scope of the world-building, the political machinations. It's a grand opera, almost. And honestly, Timothée Chalamet does his best with what he's given. It's Herbert's writing that's…distant. Speaker_1: Grand opera that bored me stiff for two and a half hours, then. Look, I appreciate world-building, I do. But what’s the point if I don’t *care* who's gettin’ stabbed in the back in this fancy desert world? Kvothe, though…you feel his struggle. His arrogance, his loss. Rothfuss makes you invest. And that’s why it’s so infuriatin’ he hasn't finished the series! Speaker_2: (Smiling) Tell me about it. The waiting is agony. I’m on chapter five of a reread, just trying to keep the embers alive. But moving away from tortured fantasy protagonists…what have you been reading *besides* lamenting unfinished series? I know you were ploughing through that collection of short stories by Angela Carter. Speaker_1: Oh, she’s brilliant, isn’t she? Utterly brilliant. Completely bonkers, but brilliant. Like, “The Bloody Chamber” - re-tellin’ Bluebeard as proper gothic horror with a feminist edge. It’s just…so sharp. And the language! It's all so lush and disturbing at the same time. Makes you think about fairytales in a completely different way. Speaker_2: Sounds intense. I’ve meant to read some Carter for ages. I've been… mostly technical papers lately, unfortunately. Although, I did manage to get through a biography of Isambard Kingdom Brunel. Fascinating man. Proper Victorian engineering genius. Speaker_1: Brunel, aye? Always a good shout. Practical, ya know? Not like all this existential ponderin’ in books. Speaking of practical…I’m starvin’. Did you remember to get those pasties from Greggs? I was thinking a steak and onion one would really hit the spot. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Of course I did. I *knew* that was coming. Three steak and onion, one sausage roll, and a jam doughnut. The usual. They’re in the boot, with the shopping. You’re such a creature of habit. Speaker_1: Hey, don’t knock it! Greggs is a national treasure. And a steak pasty is a culinary *experience*. Especially after a particularly underwhelming film like *Dune*. It’s a proper comfort food. Better than fancy foams and microgreens any day. Speaker_2: I’ll concede Greggs does a very good steak pasty. Though, I did take you to that new tapas place last week, and you seemed to enjoy the patatas bravas. Speaker_1: I did! Proper tasty, they were. But it's a different vibe, isn’t it? Greggs is… reliable. A constant. Tapas is for treatin' yerself. Like watchin’ a really good film with characters ya actually care about. Speaker_2: Fair enough. Well, we've got pasties, a potentially traumatizing discussion about *Dune* behind us, and a drive to your mum's. Sounds like a good evening to me.

Speaker_2: It was for Princess Luna! She’s got a dragon, but he’s a friendly dragon. He helps her fight the bad guys. Speaker_3: And it needs a moat! A really big moat with…with crocodiles! And a drawbridge! Speaker_1: A drawbridge and crocodiles. Excellent additions. It sounds like a very clever princess and a very sophisticated defence system. You know, when *I* was little, I didn’t have all this Lego. We had… well, we had my Dad’s old typewriter. Speaker_2: A what-er? Speaker_1: A typewriter! Speaker_1: We’ll see, love. Maybe. Right now, it’s getting late. And all this talk about computers and princesses and typewriters is making *me* tired. How about we all snuggle under the duvet and I read you another chapter of your story? Speaker_2: Ooh, yes! The one about the brave knight! Speaker_3: And the dragon! The friendly dragon! Speaker_1: (Smiling) Exactly. The brave knight and the friendly dragon. Alright then. Let's turn off the lights and get cosy. It’s been lovely chatting with you both. You’re both such brilliant storytellers, you know that?

Speaker_1: … honestly, Arthur, you look like you’ve slept in your clothes. Not a criticism, mind, just an observation. You’ve got a bit of, well, everything on that jumper. Jam, I reckon? Now, have you tried the blueberries? I got them from that new farm shop near Haworth. Proper fruit farm, you know, not just supermarket stuff. They were picking them yesterday. Speaker_2: Blueberries are lovely, thank you. Reminds me of a job I did near Kent, years ago. Massive fruit farms there. Strawberries as big as your fist. Though, you know, efficiency’s gone out of it. Everything’s standardized, pre-packaged… less flavour. Like those deserted medieval villages we were talking about last time. All planned, neat, then… gone. Speaker_1: Aye, that’s a thought. Makes you wonder, doesn’t it? All that effort, all that life, just… vanished. I was reading about one near Ilkley, Wharram Percy. Completely empty now, aside from sheep. It’s that roadworks that get me though, same as it’s been for years! They started near the bypass last autumn, still digging! You'd think they were tunneling to Australia. Speaker_2: Roadworks are the bane of my existence. Always disrupting things. Engineer’s perspective, I suppose. Though most of the time they seem to be employing people who’ve never actually *seen* a road before. Speaking of disruptions, have you had much junk mail lately? I’m drowning in it. Offers for funeral plans, insurance… It’s like they’re anticipating my demise. Speaker_1: Oh, don’t even start me on the junk mail! It’s terrible. And the phone! Constant calls about PPI… it’s exhausting. I barely answer it anymore. Honestly, it's enough to make you want to move to a desert island. More coffee? I made a fresh pot. And I've got some mint growing on the windowsill – fancy a leaf in your brew? Speaker_2: That sounds lovely, Doreen. Mint coffee, now that's something. You've got a good touch with herbs, you do. My late wife, bless her, tried growing them. Said she couldn't tell a basil from a bindweed. (Pause) It’s queer, isn’t it? Getting to this age. All your friends are either complaining about their knees or talking about… well, the inevitable. Speaker_1: (Softly) It is, Arthur. It is. We’re all getting on a bit, aren't we? Still, better to have a good moan over a cup of coffee and some jam-covered jumper, than sit in silence. Now, about ANON’s house… Have you spoken to the estate agent again this week? Speaker_2: Aye, I did. Still no firm offers. They say the market’s a bit sluggish. Apparently, everyone's holding out for a bargain. It's frustrating. She wanted it sold quickly, you know? It’s eating away at me, the thought of it standing empty. That house held a lot of memories. Speaker_1: It did. A lovely house, even if it *is* a bit draughty. Don’t worry too much, Arthur. It’ll go eventually. In the meantime, we’ll just keep having breakfast, and you can keep getting jam on your jumper. Now, more blueberries? Before I eat them all myself.

Speaker_1: … honestly, I just think she’s overdoing it with the vitamins, David. Honestly, a woman her age needs a bit of common sense, not a whole pharmacy tucked into her handbag! Remember that rash you got last year from that fancy serum? Speaker_1: That was different! That was a reaction, this is… deliberate sliminess. Honestly. Still, she was going on about how fabulous she feels, anticipating New Year’s. She's already planned a whole weekend in Brighton. Can you imagine, Brighton in January? Speaker_3: (Looking up from her phone) Sounds bracing. Though, Mum, Brighton's got some really good vegan restaurants now. Might be worth a trip ourselves, actually. I saw a post on Facebook about one called Terre à Terre… apparently, it's unbelievable. Speaker_1: Facebook, always Facebook, Tilly. Honestly, you’d think you live in there. And Brighton’s alright, if you don’t mind the seagulls trying to steal your chips. I'm worried about getting there myself, though. Remembering the directions is a nightmare. Last time we went, I ended up driving round in circles near Crawley. Speaker_2: (Smiling) I’ll navigate, darling. I’ve finally mastered using Google Maps on my phone. Though, I still prefer a proper map, if I’m honest. Feels more… secure. It's like relying on a compass instead of GPS. Speaker_1: Secure? David, you nearly drove us into a field in Devon using a proper map last summer! Honestly, you and your “sense of direction”. It's a myth! Speaker_2: That was… a misinterpretation of the contours, Mum. A slight misinterpretation. Anyway, speaking of feeling good, did you take your blood pressure tablets this morning, love? Speaker_1: Oh, don’t start lecturing me! Yes, I did. First thing. Honestly, you sound like a doctor. And Tilly, no judging. I had a little glass of prosecco with lunch. It’s nearly New Year! Speaker_3: No judgment! Just concerned. It interacts with your medication, doesn't it? And speaking of prosecco, I got you both something for Christmas… Actually, it's more for Mum. It’s that lavender hand cream you like – the one from the little shop in Ashford. Speaker_1: Oh, Tilly, you shouldn't have! That *is* lovely. Honestly, you remember everything. I did mention it once, didn't I? It's the only thing that stops my hands from cracking in this weather. Though, Dizzy's been sneaking a sniff of it too. The daft dog thinks it's a new toy! Speaker_2: (Laughing) He's a character, that one. Still haven’t forgiven him for eating my slippers last Christmas. Honestly, the audacity! Speaker_3: He's just a puppy at heart, Dad. He’s got a sensitive nose. Though, talking of presents, did you manage to get that… thing… for Mum, Dad? The back massager? Speaker_2: (Clears throat) Er, well… it’s on order. Apparently, there’s a slight delay with delivery. Something about “global shipping issues”. It'll get here. Speaker_1: (Raises an eyebrow) “On order”? Oh, David. You left it to the last minute, didn't you? Honestly, you’re always like this. Never plan ahead! Speaker_2: I planned! I just… underestimated the demand for back massagers in December. It’s a popular gift, Mum. Apparently.

It pays the bills, which is the main thing right now. Rent in London is just… obscene. I'm seriously considering moving back to Kent, you know? Mum keeps hinting she's got a spare room, and honestly, the thought of having a garden again… and not having to remortgage myself every month… It's tempting. Speaker_2: Back to Ashford? That’s a big shift. Though, I can see the appeal. I'm lucky, I’m still living at home while I finish my Masters. The privilege is *real*. Although, even with that, money's tight. This part-time survey programming is… not exactly lucrative. It's just to keep me afloat and away from asking the Bank of Mum and Dad for everything. Speaker_1: You’re doing a Masters though, that’s brilliant! What is it in again? Speaker_2: Computational Linguistics. It’s fascinating, but terrifying. The stuff they’re asking us to learn about AI… it's a bit much sometimes. It feels like everything's changing so fast. Makes me wonder if there *will* be jobs in my field by the time I graduate. Speaker_1: Don't even get me started on AI taking over jobs! My boss was talking about using an AI writer for some of the simpler stuff. The south coast to London train robbery. I'm heading up to see my sister in Manchester next month. Similar story. Have you managed to get out much yourself lately? I’ve seen some cheap flights.

Before you got promoted and suddenly had a company car? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Right, when I was still driving that… well, let's just say it was a character-building vehicle. The Fiesta. Speaker_1: Exactly! And now *my* reliable car is becoming a money pit. I’m trying to figure out if it’s worth getting it serviced, or if it’s just throwing good money after bad. It's an old Volvo, you know they can be deceptively expensive to fix. Speaker_2: Definitely get a quote. A good mechanic can tell you straight. Maybe it’s just something small.
