Though these petrol prices are crippling, aren't they? Getting to and from Birmingham is costing a fortune. Reminds me of the seventies, queues at the petrol stations and all. Speaker_1: It is ridiculous, isn’t it? I’m trying to cycle more, but Solihull isn’t exactly cycle-friendly. They *talk* about improving infrastructure, but it’s slow going. I’m seriously considering looking into getting a small electric car, but they're still so expensive. Thinking about a trip to France next year, and the cost of getting the car on the ferry… it all adds up. Speaker_2: France? Lovely! I haven’t been abroad in… oh, goodness, must be ten years now. Used to go to Spain with my husband, every year. He loved the heat. Miss that, to be honest. This weather we're getting now… it’s all over the place. Flooding one minute, drought the next. It worries me, it really does. What kind of world are we leaving for the grandchildren? Speaker_1: Exactly! It's terrifying. I try to bring it up in class, with the younger ones, the importance of environmental responsibility, but it’s hard to get through. They’re overwhelmed by everything, you know? It feels so enormous. My niece, Lily, she’s just started university, studying Marine Biology. She’s fiercely dedicated, but even *she* seems discouraged sometimes. Speaker_2: That’s good she’s studying something like that, at least. Science needs bright minds. My grandson, wee Jamie, he's doing well in school. Wants to be an engineer, apparently. Says he wants to design something to… clean the oceans, was it? It’s lovely to hear them having ambition. Though, getting them through university…that’s the expensive part, isn’t it? Student loans are a nightmare. Speaker_1: A complete nightmare. I feel so lucky I managed to get a postgraduate loan, but it’s a weight hanging over me. I sometimes wonder if it was worth it, financially speaking. The job satisfaction is good, though. Seeing a student finally *get* a grammatical concept, or write a really good essay… that's rewarding. Speaker_2: That sounds lovely. It's good to have a job you enjoy. I just feel… a bit stuck sometimes. The ushering is alright, pays the bills, but it's not exactly a career, is it? My husband, God rest him, he was a carpenter. Proper skilled tradesman. They don't seem to value that kind of thing anymore. Everything's about qualifications. Speaker_1: It’s a shame. There’s something very satisfying about working with your hands, creating something tangible. My dad was a builder, and he always said the same thing. This emphasis on academic routes for everyone just isn’t realistic, or fair. It leaves so many people feeling… left behind. Speaker_2: Aye. Left behind. Well, it’s getting late

Speaker_1: …and honestly, that's what it feels like, doesn’t it? Just…peaceful. Not needing anything extra. Though, a little more sleep wouldn't go amiss! Speaker_2: (Giggles) Mummy, if we had *loads* of money, could we buy a bouncy castle that’s as big as the garden? Speaker_3: And a robot dinosaur! A really, really big one that breathes *fire*! Speaker_1: (Smiling) Oh, you two. A bouncy castle the size of the garden… that *would* be something. And a fire-breathing dinosaur. Right. Where would we even *put* a fire-breathing dinosaur? Speaker_2: In the garden! With the bouncy castle! Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Logical. But you know, having loads of money wouldn’t automatically make us happy, would it? Speaker_3: Why not? Money buys you everything! Ben at school got a new Lego spaceship because his dad has money. Speaker_1: That’s true, money *can* buy things. But it doesn't buy happiness, sweetheart. It buys…well, things. Like Lego spaceships, and maybe even a bouncy castle. But happiness comes from different places. From spending time together, like we are now. From reading a good book. From helping someone else. Speaker_2: Like when we gave Mrs. Higgins flowers? She looked really smiley. Speaker_1: Exactly! That made *you* feel good, didn't it? That’s happiness. It's a feeling. Speaker_3: But…the dinosaur! Speaker_1: (Laughing) The dinosaur is a lovely thought, honestly. But imagine having all the money in the world and feeling lonely. Or having all the toys but no one to play with. That wouldn’t be very fun, would it? Speaker_2: No. That sounds…sad. Speaker_1: It would be. You know, there's a little rhyme I learned when I was little. Do you want to hear it? Speaker_3: Ooh, yes! A rhyme about dinosaurs? Speaker_1: Not *about* dinosaurs, but it’s good. “Money can’t buy you laughter, it can’t buy you cheer, it can’t buy you a sunny day to chase away a tear.” Speaker_2: (Repeating) “Money can’t buy you laughter…” That’s a good one! Speaker_3: Can it buy you chocolate? Speaker_1: (Smiling) Yes, it can buy you chocolate. But eating too much chocolate doesn’t make you *happy* for very long, does it? It might for a little bit, but then you feel a bit…yucky. Speaker_2: True! I felt yucky after I ate all my biscuits last week. Speaker_1: See? So, happiness isn’t about *having* lots of things, or lots of money. It’s about…feeling grateful for what we *do* have. Like a warm house, and each other. And maybe...a slightly smaller, non-fire-breathing dinosaur toy. Speaker_3: Okay. A small one. But it *has* to roar! Speaker_1: It absolutely has to roar. We can look for a roaring dinosaur tomorrow. For now, how about we build a fort? That always makes me happy. Speaker_2: YES! A fort! Can we use all the cushions? Speaker_1: All the cushions! Let's go! And maybe, just maybe, while we're building, we can think about all the things that make us happy that don’t cost a single penny.

Speaker_1: … honestly, it just feels a bit pointless, doesn’t it? Like, Mrs. Davies keeps going on about ‘future-proofing’ our choices, but how can you *possibly* know what jobs will even *be* around in ten years? It's not like my grandad, knowing he’d stay a mechanic all his life. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. My dad’s massively into investment now, keeps talking about ‘disruptive technologies’. Which basically means he watches videos about Elon Musk and thinks he’s got the next big idea. He was on about quantum computing the other day. I just nodded and pretended to understand. Speaker_1: Quantum… what now? Sounds terrifyingly complicated. Though, I suppose that’s the point, isn't it? Something new all the time. It's just… overwhelming. I was thinking maybe something with engineering. You know, actually *making* stuff. But even then, it’s all AI assisted design now, isn’t it? Will there be any actual *designers* left? Speaker_2: Probably. But they’ll be coding the AI, I guess. My cousin, Liam, he’s doing a foundation year in computer science. He's completely obsessed with patents. Apparently, someone invented a self-folding laundry basket and made a fortune. A *laundry basket*, Sam! Speaker_1: No way! Seriously? That’s… ridiculous. And brilliant. I mean, who thinks of that? Though, thinking about it, patenting stuff sounds like a headache. All the legal bits, making sure no one steals your idea. Speaker_2: He says it’s surprisingly complex. Loads of loopholes, international law, all that. But the rewards can be huge. He's actually got an idea for a better bike lock – one that uses facial recognition. Slightly terrifying, maybe, but apparently, bike theft is a massive problem. Speaker_1: That’s…actually quite good. Safer. Still, feels a bit Big Brother-ish. Speaking of big… have you been reading about China lately? It feels like they’re just… everywhere. Economically, technologically. Speaker_2: Yeah, my geography teacher's been banging on about it. The Belt and Road initiative, all that. Apparently, they’re investing massively in infrastructure all over Africa and Asia. They're aiming to control everything. It’s kinda scary. Speaker_1: Scary and… impressive. They're building things at a scale we haven’t seen since, well, probably the Romans. And they’re not messing about with ethical considerations like we are. They just *do* things. Speaker_2: Exactly! Dad reckons that’s why they’re winning. No red tape. Easier to get things off the ground. He's been looking into investing in some Chinese tech companies, but Mum put her foot down. Says it’s too risky. Speaker_1: Risky, yeah, and… ethically questionable. I mean, all the reports about forced labour and stuff. It's complicated. It feels like the whole world is changing so fast. Like everything we thought we knew is going to be… different. Speaker_2: Different, and probably more competitive. That’s why my Dad keeps going on about investment. Says we need to be thinking about building passive income streams, to safeguard against…everything. Honestly, it's exhausting just listening to him. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. Passive income streams. It sounds like something out of a dystopian novel. Maybe I’ll just stick to trying to invent a self-cleaning classroom. Now *that’s* a market ripe for disruption. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Now *that* is a good idea, Sam. Patent that immediately. We could be millionaires! Though, knowing Upton Court, they’d probably just make us clean it anyway.

Speaker_1: … honestly, I just think Darren’s getting a bit too confident. He was practically showing off on that red run this morning, carving these huge turns, and then nearly took out little Timmy Perkins! Honestly, the man. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, Darren. He *is* a bit of a show-off, isn't he? But bless him, he’s enjoying himself. Timmy’s fine, apparently just a bit winded. Did you see old Mr. Henderson practically doing the splits trying to avoid him? That was almost better than Darren’s actual skiing. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Oh, I did! Poor man. He's nearly eighty, that fella. I felt terrible laughing, truly. But it was… unexpectedly funny. Anyway, I’m worried about Mum and Dad trying the blue run tomorrow. Dad hasn't skied in *years*. Speaker_2: They’ll be alright. Ben said he'd stick with them, and he’s a very sensible skier. You know, he’s really taken to it. I didn’t expect that. He always said he preferred snowboarding. Speaker_1: He did, didn’t he? Funny how things change. It’s nice seeing him enjoy something with Mum and Dad. It’s… it’s nice seeing them all together, to be honest. We don’t get enough of that back home. Everyone’s so busy. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. Work, kids, life… it just sweeps you along. That’s why I insisted on this trip. A full week, just us, away from everything. Although, ‘away from everything’ doesn’t mean ‘away from Auntie Brenda’s constant updates on the cat’s digestion, does it? Speaker_1: (Groans) Oh, don’t even *mention* Fluffy. I got three photos of his… output… this morning. Three! I’ve muted her WhatsApp group for the week. She’ll forgive me. Probably. Speaker_2: Good. You deserve peace. Listen, about Friday… Are you still happy to swap rooms with me and Michael? He’s already complaining about the noise coming from the bar downstairs, and I think a bit of peace and quiet will do him good. Speaker_1: No problem at all. It’s easier for me, honestly. I need to do a bit of work on Saturday morning – some proofreading for that American client. Lower floor means better wifi, apparently. That hotel’s wifi is patchy at best. Speaker_2: Good thinking. Actually, speaking of work… How’s things going with that new marketing gig? The one for the estate agents? Speaker_1: It’s… challenging. They want everything yesterday, and they have very specific ideas about *everything*, none of which are very good, frankly. But it pays the bills. And it’s mostly remote, which is ideal. I just wish they’d realise a Facebook post with a blurry picture of a garden isn’t going to sell a five-bedroom detached. Speaker_2: Oh, you’re dealing with amateurs. You should tell them! You're brilliant at what you do. Remember that campaign you did for the bakery last year? That was genius. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Thanks, love. You always know what to say. It’s just… draining sometimes, explaining basic marketing principles to people who think a hashtag is a type of hat. Speaker_2: Well, enjoy your lunch, and try not to think about estate agents or cat poo. Let’s just enjoy the mountains, the wine, and the fact we’ve managed to escape for a week. And maybe subtly warn Darren to take it easy on the slopes. Speaker_1: Definitely. And maybe hide my phone from Brenda. Another glass of wine?

Speaker_1: …and honestly, Arthur, I just don’t see why you keep getting through strings so quickly. Are you *really* hitting them that hard anymore? It’s not like you’re competing at Wimbledon, is it? Speaker_2: (Chuckles, a slight South of England lilt noticeable) Now, now, Margaret, don't be like that. It's not about hitting hard, it's about the… the tension, I think. And the frame flexing. It’s a combination. Remember Old Man Hemmings at the club? He said the newer rackets are just… less forgiving. Speaker_1: Hemmings said a lot of things. Mostly about the price of biscuits in the clubhouse. Anyway, we’re talking solutions. The cable ties are a temporary fix, and frankly, quite unsightly. I’m still leaning towards the reinforced grommet system. Perhaps with a small, rubber washer in there too, to absorb some of the shock. Speaker_2: Grommets, yes. Good. But sourcing them… that’s the problem. Finding them in the right size, consistently. And the cost. We’re trying to keep this accessible, remember? The whole point is not to rip people off. A fiver for a repair, maximum. Speaker_1: A fiver is ambitious. Especially if we’re talking about replacing several grommets *and* restringing. Maybe six, then? And we need to factor in the cost of the string itself. I was looking online, a decent roll of badminton string is… well, it’s not cheap these days. Speaker_2: Right. And then there’s the question of positioning. Where exactly do we reinforce? Just the main string holes? Or are we thinking… a wider support structure? It almost feels like building a mini… fleet of supports. Speaker_1: (Slightly exasperated) A *fleet*, Arthur? Really? That’s a rather dramatic way to describe a few grommets. Though, I suppose you’re picturing a squadron of tiny reinforcements defending against breakage. Speaker_2: (Laughing) It just… came to me! Anyway, and speaking of reinforcements… (He pauses, fiddling with the clippers). Sorry, just need to… adjust the guard. Now, this is where it gets tricky. I'm attempting a little tidy up. It's been getting a bit long, you see. Speaker_1: (A small yelp) Arthur! Careful! That’s awfully close to my ear! Oh dear, you’ve… you’ve nipped it! Just a tiny bit, thankfully. Speaker_2: Oh, blast! I am *so* sorry, Margaret! It’s the light, you see. And trying to concentrate on grommets and fleets at the same time is a bit much, even for me. Speaker_1: (Rubbing her ear gently) It stings! And… oh, look. You’ve also taken a stripe off my hair. It looked rather fetching, that stripe. Speaker_2: (Looking horrified) Good heavens! I… I didn’t realise! I’ll try to even it out. Perhaps a slightly shorter length all over? We could market it as a ‘Badminton Repair Specialist’ haircut! Speaker_1: (Scoffs) Don’t be ridiculous. We’re not marketing a botched haircut alongside badminton racket repairs. Although… perhaps that’s the angle? “Get your racket *and* your hair fixed!” No. Bad idea. Speaker_2: Maybe not. But we *do* need a marketing strategy. Dragons’ Den, perhaps? Imagine, presenting our grommet-fleet system to Deborah Meaden… Speaker_1: Dragons’ Den? Arthur, you're dreaming! They’d laugh us out of the den. "A fiver for a racket repair? Using cable ties? And a hastily constructed grommet network?" No. Besides, I don’t fancy getting grilled by those sharks. We’re better off starting small, targeting the local clubs. Steppingstone Primary, maybe. They have a very enthusiastic badminton club, and it’s mostly younger

Speaker_1: …No, no, I’m tellin’ ya, it weren’t right, see? All that blue. Far too much blue. Reminded me o’ bein’ seasick, truth be told. Though I 'aven’t *been* seasick, mind you. Just the *feel* of it. Like lookin’ at a storm brewin’ over Breydon Water. Depressin', that's what it was. Speaker_2: Oh, Arthur, you always say that about modern art! Anything that isn’t a nice landscape with sheep gets a bad rap from you. You liked that Turner exhibition, didn’t you? Plenty of blue in *that*! Speaker_1: Turner were different, Elsie. He knew 'is colour. He painted the *light*, he did. This…this was just a load o’ splodges. And the young lady, our Sarah, she's tellin' me it's expressin' the artist's inner turmoil. Inner turmoil? Sounds like ‘e needed a good cup o’ tea and a lie-down, if you ask me. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Dad, it's often about communicating feelings that are difficult to put into words. It's not necessarily about representing something *real*. It's about evoking a response in the viewer. The artist, Anya Petrova, apparently went through a really difficult period when she was creating that series. Speaker_1: Evokin’ a response? It evoked a desire for a biscuit, that’s what it evoked! A nice digestive. Now that's somethin' worthwhile. Speaker_4: It’s interesting, isn't it, how subjective art is? I actually quite liked the intensity of the blue, the way it dominated the canvas. It felt…claustrophobic, almost. Which, if Sarah’s right about the artist’s experiences, makes sense. Speaker_2: I thought it was quite striking, actually. A bit much for the lounge, mind you, but striking. And Sarah’s a clever girl, she studies this sort of thing. She'd know. Speaker_3: Anya’s work is rooted in Abstract Expressionism, so it’s intentionally non-representational. It aims to create an emotional resonance directly, bypassing the need for recognisable imagery. Think Rothko, but a bit more…visceral. Speaker_1: Rothko? Sounds like a plumber. Visceral? What does *that* even mean? Speaker_4: (Smiling) It means it affects you on a gut level, Dad. It's a strong, intuitive reaction. It's not about thinking about it, it’s about *feeling* it. Speaker_1: Well, my gut told me it needed a frame with a good strong border, maybe somethin' oak. And a nice bit o’ floral paper behind it to cheer it up. Speaker_2: Arthur! You'd ruin it! You’d completely miss the point. Speaker_3: It’s okay, Dad. You don't *have* to like it. Art is meant to challenge you, make you think, even if it's just to decide you don't like it. The important thing is that it makes you *feel* something. Speaker_4: Absolutely. And it's good to talk about it. That's the point of family visits, isn't it? – sharing perspectives and…slightly exasperating each other. Speaker_1: (Grumbling) Exasperatin’ me? I'm just tryin' to be polite! I don't want to offend the artist, but honestly, a bit of colour wouldn't go amiss. And a sheep. All art needs a sheep, if you ask me. Speaker_2: (Patting his hand) There, there, Arthur. More tea? And maybe a digestive will make that blue look a bit brighter. Speaker_3: I think she's onto something there, Dad. A digestive is always a good idea. Speaker_4: Definitely. Though perhaps not *in front* of the abstract expressionism.

Speaker_1: … honestly, I just don’t *get* her. Like, posting that selfie with the filter that makes you look like a cartoon cat? Seriously? It’s Gemma, not Garfield. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, stirring her wine) Oh, bless her. Teenage regression, I reckon. She’s probably dealing with something. Though, yeah, aesthetically… questionable. You still on about the hen do stuff? Speaker_1: It’s not just the hen do! It’s *everything*. She’s constantly fishing for compliments, and then gets offended if you don’t gush enough. I spent an hour helping her pick an outfit for Dave’s work party and then she just said ‘It’s okay, I guess.’ *Okay*?! Speaker_2: Harsh. People are weird, Liv. You’re a project coordinator, you deal with weird all day. Remember Mr. Henderson and his obsession with staplers? Speaker_1: That’s different! Staplers are objectively fascinating. This is…performative suffering. Anyway, enough about the drama of Gemma. Work was a nightmare today. Old man Peterson decided *now* is the time to restructure the entire filing system. The *entire* thing. Speaker_2: Oh, you poor thing. Sounds… thrilling. I had a patient today who tried to convince me she was a teapot. A full-on, spout-and-handle teapot. Speaker_1: (Eyes widening) No way! Did you… did you offer her a biscuit? Speaker_2: (Laughing) I was tempted! Protocol says de-escalation, not catering to delusions. It’s exhausting, honestly. You deal with the filing, I deal with the teapots. It’s a good balance. Although, sometimes I think Peterson’s filing system *is* a delusion. Speaker_1: It honestly is. And the language people use in emails! “Per my last email…” Who talks like that? It’s so…aggressive-passive. It’s like they’re trying to subtly assert dominance through grammar. Speaker_2: Stop. You’re going down a linguistic rabbit hole. Remember last week when you spent twenty minutes ranting about the misuse of ‘literally’? Speaker_1: It's important! It *means* actually! Not figuratively! It's the downfall of civilisation, I tell you. Right, I need to do the dishes. I’ve been putting it off all week. Speaker_2: Procrastination station central, is our kitchen. Honestly, it's a hazard. I tripped over that box of your craft supplies again this morning. Speaker_1: Sorry! I really need to sort that out. I swear, I’ll do it tomorrow. After I’ve organised Peterson’s filing system in my head. And analysed the etymological roots of ‘literally.’ Speaker_2: (Smiling) You’re hopeless. Look, I’m knackered. Long shift. Fancy ordering a takeaway? Pizza? We could watch something dreadful. Anything to distract from teapots and aggressive email signatures. Speaker_1: Ooh, yes! Pizza sounds amazing. And dreadful TV is my specialty. Maybe that new reality show everyone’s talking about? The one where they try to live off-grid in Wales? Speaker_2: Perfect. Disaster tourism at its finest. Let me just check my phone for deals… And you, my friend, can stare forlornly at the washing up for five more minutes. You deserve it. Speaker_1: Five minutes, tops. Then Operation Clean Kitchen commences… eventually. Speaker_2: (Sighs happily) That’s the spirit. Now, pepperoni or Margherita? This is a serious decision.

Speaker_1: … honestly, the sheer volume of emails I sifted through today was ridiculous. Mr. Henderson decided *everyone* needs to be cc’d on *everything*. It's like he thinks transparency equals drowning in admin. And then Sheila wanted me to book her a ‘wellness retreat’ in Bali. Bali! Like she’s stressed dealing with stationery orders. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, taking a sip of his beer) Sounds like a typical Tuesday for you, then. Still, Bali sounds nice. You deserve a bit of Bali after wrestling Henderson’s email habits. Though, knowing you, you'd spend the whole time networking and trying to sort *their* IT out. Speaker_1: (Scoffs) Don’t even. And it's not just the work, it's… all of it. The school run, remembering Amelia has recorder practice, making sure your mum's got her shopping… I feel like a logistical operation. Sometimes I just want to light a cigarette and stare into space. Speaker_2: Now, now. We talked about the cigarettes. Remember what Dr. Davies said? Your lungs aren’t getting any younger, love. And honestly, you're much nicer to be around *without* the constant craving looks. Want another glass of wine instead? Helps with the ‘logistical operation’ feeling. Speaker_1: (Sighs) Fine. Wine it is. But it's a temporary fix, isn’t it? It doesn’t actually *solve* anything. It's a vice, pure and simple. Like Henderson’s need to CC everyone. It’s… illogical. Speaker_2: Illogical? That’s a strong word. Maybe it's not illogical, it's just… lacking common sense. There’s a difference, you know. My old boss, Bernard, was brilliant with code – a genuine genius. But ask him to parallel park? Utter chaos. Highly intelligent, zero common sense. Speaker_1: That's true, I suppose. Intelligence isn't the same as being… well, sensible. It feels like a lot of people mistake the two. Especially with all this talk about ‘disruption’ and ‘innovation’ – sometimes you just need to use a bit of good old-fashioned common sense. Speaker_2: Exactly! It’s the same when we were in Spain last year, wasn’t it? That woman lecturing us about ‘cultural sensitivity’ while simultaneously complaining about how ‘backward’ their lunchtimes were. Speaker_1: (Grimaces) Oh, *her*. Honestly! “They shouldn’t rest for two hours in the middle of the day, it impacts productivity!” It's their culture! And a perfectly lovely one, I thought. It just feels like some people think their way is the *only* way, and any deviation is a failing. It's almost… anti-feminist in a weird way. Imposing one standard on everyone. Speaker_2: Anti-feminist? How so? Speaker_1: Well, isn't it about respecting choice? If Spanish women *choose* to value that afternoon rest, to prioritise family time… isn’t criticising that just subtly saying their choices are less valuable? It’s the same patronising tone sometimes used to dismiss women who *do* choose to be stay-at-home mothers. It's all connected, isn’t it? This idea that there's only one path to ‘success’. Speaker_2: Hmm. That’s… a really interesting point, actually. I hadn’t thought of it like that. I always saw feminism as about equal opportunities, not dictating what women *should* do with those opportunities. Speaker_1: It is, but it’s about more than that, isn't it? It’s about empowering women to make their *own* choices, without being judged. It's being allowed, and even encouraged, to prioritise different things. You know, sometimes I just fancy a quiet evening in, a glass of wine, and not having to solve the world's problems. Is that so terrible? Speaker_2: (Putting his arm around her) Absolutely

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the sheer volume of mud! I swear, Leo, you looked like you’d been wrestling a pig. A very happy pig, admittedly. Speaker_3: (Giggles) I *was* near the pigs! A little one licked my hand! It was slobbery. Speaker_2: Mine didn’t lick me! I petted a sheep, though. A fluffy one. It smelled… farmy. Speaker_1: ‘Farmy’ is a good description, actually. It wasn’t quite the idyllic countryside scene I’d envisioned, more…robust. Still, you two seemed to really enjoy it. Did you tell your teachers about the pigs and sheep at school today? Speaker_3: I told Mrs. Davies! She said pigs are very intelligent animals. She asked if I’d learned anything about their food. Speaker_2: I told Miss Evans. She said sheep need shearing, or they get too hot. But Thomas kept talking about tractors and wouldn’t let anyone else speak. Speaker_1: (Sighs gently) Thomas, darling, were you perhaps… dominating the conversation again? We talked about using our listening ears, remember? Speaker_3: He always does that! He talks and talks and talks. Speaker_2: And he makes silly faces when Miss Evans is trying to read. Speaker_1: Right. Okay. We'll have a little chat later about remembering to share the floor, shall we? It's important to let other people have a turn. It’s not just polite, it’s… it’s a skill, actually. Thinking about how others feel and letting them contribute. It’s something I teach *all* the time at school. Funny how hard it is to put into practice sometimes, isn’t it? Speaker_3: Is it like teaching grown-ups? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Sometimes, Leo, it absolutely is. Now, back to the farm. You both had a good lunch, didn’t you? Those sausage rolls were disappearing at a rate of knots. Speaker_2: I had two! And a juice box. And a biscuit! Speaker_1: That's a lot of fuel for farm-exploring. I was quite pleased you both ate something substantial. I’d packed loads, bracing myself for the ‘I'm not hungry’ chorus. Speaker_3: I was hungry! Running around with the pigs makes you hungry. Can we go again next weekend? Speaker_1: Next weekend’s already booked with Grandma and Grandpa. But we can definitely think about another farm trip soon. Actually, I was thinking we could have a movie night on Saturday. I’ve got that new Wallace and Gromit DVD. Speaker_2: Oh! The one with the sheep? Speaker_1: The very same! Although, knowing you two, you’ll probably spend the entire film re-enacting the sheep escaping. Speaker_3: Maybe! That’s a really funny bit! Speaker_1: It is. And afterwards, maybe we can build a farm out of LEGO. We’ve got enough animals to populate a whole county. Although, I suspect the arguments over who gets to be the farmer will commence immediately. Speaker_2: I want to be the farmer! I'm good at looking after things. Speaker_3: No, *I* want to be the farmer! I know all about tractors! And pigs! Speaker_1: (Smiling, a touch weary) Alright, alright. We'll negotiate. Perhaps we'll have two farms. That always solves everything, doesn’t it? Now, who wants another biscuit? Just…not covered in mud this time, please.

Speaker_1: … honestly, it’s just so satisfying, isn’t it? The click-clack of the needles. Proper mindful, like. I’m trying to do a Fair Isle pattern, though, and it’s…ambitious. Especially after just finishing that plain garter stitch scarf for me mam. Felt a bit basic after all the research I’ve been doing for work, if I’m honest. Apparently, he was convinced Horace, the hamster, was poorly and needed ‘warming up’. Thankfully, the mother walked in before anything actually *happened*. It was a right kerfuffle. Speaker_1: Warming up? Good Lord. Poor little beast. Makes you wonder what goes on in these youngsters’ ‘eads. Reminds me o’ when I was a lad, we tried to make a rocket out of a jam jar and gunpowder… nearly blew me shed to smithereens, it did. Father weren’t best pleased. Speaker_2: You and explosions, Arthur! It’s a wonder you made it to seventy-eight. Though, honestly, David, a hamster… it’s just so bizarre. Nowadays, they all want these fancy computer-controlled ones. No soul in it, I reckon. You don't *feel* the wood when you’re letting a computer do all the work. Speaker_3: There’s definitely something to be said for the traditional skills, Arthur. Though the precision of the modern ones is undeniable. It’s just a different approach. Do you still have all your turning chisels, then? Speaker_1: Most of 'em, aye. Packed away in the shed. Bit rusty, I’ll grant you. Haven’t touched ‘em properly since me arthritis started playing up. Honestly, you’re a menace to yourself. Leave the sharpening to a professional. We don’t want to be visiting you in hospital. More quiche, David? It’s gone down a treat. Speaker_3: Certainly, Patricia. You’re a wonderful cook. And Arthur, maybe a nice, gentle wood-carving project instead of the lathe? Something a bit less…hazardous? Speaker_1: (Grumbling good-naturedly) Wood-carving? That’s for girls, David! No, no. I’ll stick to reminiscing about the old days. And worrying about youngsters trying to microwave hamsters. Speaker_1: …and honestly, the sheer arrogance of it! Charging five pence for a plastic bag. Five pence! Like it’s going to solve anything. It just feels like another little nibble at our pockets, doesn't it? Speaker_2: It’s the principle, isn’t it? They claim it’s environmental, but I bet the cost of *administering* the charge outweighs any good it does. My mum was going on about it, refusing to pay, causing a right scene at Tesco. Classic. Speaker_3: (Chuckles softly) Oh, your mother. Always a firebrand. Though, I do agree with the sentiment. It’s performative activism, really. A tiny gesture to make people *feel* like something is being done. Reminds me a bit of all this fuss over American politics. Endless bluster, very little substance. Speaker_1: Absolutely. Speaker_2: It’s horrifying, isn't it? Makes you appreciate relative stability, even with all our own little grievances. Speaking of grievances, have you seen house prices lately? Absolutely insane. We’re never going to be able to downsize to the coast at this rate. Speaker_1: Don’t even *start* me on house prices. I was looking at places for… well, for potential future scenarios. Just researching. And even a tiny little bungalow in Dorset is beyond ridiculous. It’s criminal, really. Generations priced out. Speaker_3: It's a disgrace, truly. Speaker_2: It is. Though, you always managed brilliantly, Agnes. You built that school up from almost nothing. A proper legacy. Speaker_3: Well, someone had to. Children deserve the best start, regardless of their background. Though, I sometimes wonder if I spent too much time ensuring everything was perfect and not enough time… enjoying life. Although, I did have Tibbles. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Tibbles! Oh, I remember Tibbles. Your magnificent Maine Coon. I saw that story in the news today, about the cat that wandered into a brewery and started ‘working’ as a mouser. It reminded me of Tibbles, stalking through the garden like a tiny lion. Speaker_2: (Laughing) A brewery? That's brilliant! They were giving him beer tokens as payment, apparently. Though, knowing cats, he'd probably trade them for a nap in a warm box. Speaker_3: They are remarkably practical creatures. More so than some people I’ve known. Speaking of practical, have you both been doing the cryptic crossword? I’ve been stuck on 23 down for hours. “Instrument of torture, initially withdrawn (7).” Speaker_1: Oh, *that* one! I think it’s “rackings”. R-A-C-K-I-N-G-S. “Rack” being the instrument, and "initially withdrawn" hinting at the first letters. Speaker_2: Clever! I was miles off. I was trying to work in something about banking, given the current… instability. You know, racketeering, financial racketeering. I’m clearly thinking too much about bills. Speaker_1: That’s easily done, isn’t it? It’s always looming. I had a rather frustrating conversation with the bank this morning. Something about a direct debit not going through. Honestly, navigating their automated systems is like trying to decipher mirror-writing. Speaker_3: Mirror-writing? Fascinating. Apparently, Leonardo da Vinci was quite the practitioner. A very particular way of thinking, they say. Although, I suspect it was just a habit born of left-handedness. Speaker_2: Probably. Everything’s overcomplicated these days, isn’

Speaker_1: …and honestly, the sheer volume of people at the Colosseum was just *ridiculous*. It felt less like experiencing history and more like being herded cattle. Still, Rome was lovely, though. A bit of a distraction would be perfect. Is it the one near the cathedral? Speaker_2: It is, yeah. I haven't had a proper look around Lichfield in ages. I spend so much time commuting and then just collapsing when I get home. Maybe we could grab some lunch somewhere nice afterwards? We could even go for a walk along the canal afterwards, if the weather holds. It's lovely and peaceful. Speaker_3: That sounds like a brilliant plan, Mum. Honestly, just spending the day with you both is a good distraction. I think I needed that, actually. Speaker_2: Me too. A day off is a rare treat these days. Right, well, I best get a move on and get changed. And then perhaps a quick scout for those missing swan-shaped biscuits… just in case. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Oh, Liv. You’re a treasure, you are. Let’s go and find those trinkets then, shall we? I'm glad I’m back. It’s good to be home.

Speaker_1: … honestly, Mr. Harrison is taking the mickey. Giving us three essays *and* a practical for next week? It’s ridiculous. Especially after that history test on Tuesday. I barely slept. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) A masterpiece, eh? You and your dramatic flair, Chloe. Anyway, this sandwich is… functional. Just bread and cheese. Mum clearly wasn't feeling inspired this morning. Yours look alright, Raj. Speaker_2: It's a chicken salad from Greggs. Can't go wrong, can ya? Though it’s kinda depressing that this is a highlight of the week. We’re sixth form! Shouldn’t we be, I don’t know, debating the merits of Sartre over gourmet sandwiches? Speaker_3: Speaking of depressing, did you see what happened on the news last night? That thing in…where was it? Sudan? Absolutely awful. My uncle was telling me about his time in the army, and it just… it makes you think. He wouldn't talk about specifics, just said things are never black and white. Speaker_1: My grandad was in the army. He never talked about it either. Just said it "hardened" him. Bit scary, that. It's mad to think people are dealing with that right now, while we're arguing about sandwich fillings. Speaker_2: Yeah, it’s a bit… jarring. Still, gotta focus on surviving Harrison, right? Fancy a game of Magic while we finish up? I've been testing out this new deck. Speaker_3: Ooh, yes! I need to beat you both. You’ve been gloating all week since beating me last time. Although, honestly, I think Ben in our class is secretly cheating. He *always* pulls the winning card. It's suspicious. Speaker_1: Ben? Nah. He's just lucky. Besides, he’s too busy trying to impress Prefect Johnson. Seriously, that guy thinks he's God's gift to Slough Grammar. Speaker_2: Johnson is a joke. All power, no substance. He spends more time polishing his badge than actually *doing* anything. Remember when he tried to stop Liam from wearing a band t-shirt? Called it “inappropriate attire”. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh my god, yes! The irony! He was wearing those awful argyle socks *again*. Speaking of inappropriate, have you guys seen the new season of ‘Stranger Things’? Speaker_1: Almost finished it! It’s… okay. A bit predictable, I think. Not as good as season three. Although Vecna is pretty terrifying. Speaker_2: Agreed. It’s lost a bit of its magic. I've been watching ‘Taskmaster’ instead. Greg Davies is a genius. The way he just eviscerates the contestants is brilliant. Speaker_3: Oh, Taskmaster is the best! Remember Alex Horne trying to build a bridge out of spaghetti? Legendary. Okay, enough TV chat. Raj, shuffle those cards. I’m ready for revenge! And Liam is coming to meet us after school – he said he wants to try and organise a movie night. Speaker_1: Good shout. He’s been proper quiet lately. Still reeling from…well, you know. The whole thing with Gemma. Speaker_2: Yeah, that was rough. Hopefully, a movie night will cheer him up. Anyone fancy pizza? My Dad’s taking us to that new Italian place in Windsor on Saturday, but a takeaway tonight sounds good. Speaker_3: Pizza sounds amazing. Though, let's be real, I'm still probably going to scrape a C. Have you heard anything about what Mrs. Thompson’s doing about the reading lessons? It's always stuff no one actually cares about, like Wordsworth rambling about daffodils. I mean, what’s the point? Speaker_2: Exactly! It’s all just…flowery language. And then she asks us what it *means*. Like, it's a daffodil, Mrs. Thompson. It’s yellow. Done. Speaking of pointless, have you seen Poppy Millington trying to act all mature since getting a boyfriend? Speaker_1: (laughs) Oh, don't even *start* on Poppy. She's convinced she’s in a rom-com. She keeps sighing and looking dramatically out the window. Honestly, she's trying way too hard. Remember when she tripped over her own feet in the canteen last week? Totally ruined the ‘mysterious, lovelorn’ vibe. Speaker_2: Oh my god, yes! And then blamed it on the uneven flooring! It was hilarious. It reminds me of that film, '17 Again'. Remember that? Matthew Perry turning back into a teenager? Speaker_1: Oh yeah! I love that film. Imagine Mr. Lewis, our form tutor, as the teenage version of himself. The chaos! He’d probably just spend all day eating crisps and winding everyone up. Speaker_2: (laughing) Oh, *definitely*. And trying to play pranks on Mrs. Davies. That would be brilliant. So, you reckon he’d be trying to sneak into a sixth form party then? Speaker_1: Absolutely. He’d be the first one over the fence. Although, knowing him, he’d probably get stuck. Has anyone actually figured out what’s going on with Leo and Chloe? They’ve been giving each other the *weirdest* looks all week. Speaker_2: I think Leo fancies her, but he's too terrified to actually say anything. Chloe seems completely oblivious. Or maybe she's pretending to be. She’s good at that. Remember when she pretended to like old musicals just to get Daniel to ask her out? Speaker_1: Oh, that was *genius*. Manipulative genius, but still. She's got game. Though, honestly, the whole school drama is exhausting. I just want to get through these exams and then, like, vanish for the summer. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! I’m already planning a whole summer of doing absolutely nothing. Except maybe re-watching '17 Again'. And avoiding all daffodils.

And maybe some of those salt mines I read about? Sound a bit mad, but apparently, they’re incredible. Speaker_2: The salt mines sound amazing! Maybe we should drag him to the pub with us? Force some sunlight on him? Speaker_4: Good idea. I was thinking we could try and recreate some of the *Alice in Wonderland* photos Grandad took of me when I was your age. Remember those, Leo? I had the blue dress… Speaker_3: The one with the big bow? You looked like a princess! Speaker_1: I did rather! We could do some with you two as the Mad Hatter and the Queen of Hearts.
